sections.text: To pay off a mortgage by a chosen date, work backward from the date: the monthly payment needed is the standard payment formula applied to your current balance and the months you want left. On a $265,000 balance at an assumed 6.25% with 27 years remaining, finishing in 20 years takes $1,936.96 a month instead of $1,695.16, which is $241.80 more and saves $84,360.57 of interest. Finishing in 15 years takes $2,272.17. This guide is about picking and testing a payoff date, not about extra-payment tactics, which other guides on this site cover.

items: Current principal balance, from your latest statement (not the original loan amount).
Current principal-and-interest payment. Leave out taxes and insurance in escrow, as the Mortgage Payoff Calculator does.

sections.text: The example uses a $265,000 balance, 6.25% fixed, 324 months (27 years) remaining. Rate and balance are assumptions for illustration, not a market quote. Standard payment: $1,695.16, with $284,230.91 of total interest left on the schedule. The first payment includes $1,380.21 of interest, 81.4% of the payment.

The cost of each year removed rises as the target gets shorter. Going from 27 to 26 years adds $25.25 a month, from 16 to 15 years adds $85.41, and from 11 to 10 years adds $194.26. Early years are cheap, late ones are not, so a target of 20 to 25 years may fit a budget that 10 years will not.

The rate matters less than the date. For a 15-year payoff of the same $265,000 balance, the required payment is $2,130.28 at 5.25%, $2,272.17 at 6.25% and $2,419.09 at 7.25%. A full percentage point changes the payment by roughly $140 to $150, while moving the target from 20 to 15 years changes it by $335.21. Choose the date first, then see what your rate makes of it.
Step 3: test what-ifs against your budget
If a target payment is too high, check what a fixed extra amount buys instead. Each row assumes the extra is added to the $1,695.16 payment every month from now on and applied to principal.

An amount that does not land on a round year still moves the date. Rounding the payment up from $1,695.16 to $1,700 shortens the loan by two months and saves $2,490.00 of interest, with almost no change in your budget.
Step 4: one lump sum instead of a higher payment
You can also pull the date in with a single payment now while keeping the same $1,695.16. These lump sums are what the balance must drop by today to finish on a given date.
A lump sum and a higher payment are not exclusive. Splitting the difference, for example some cash now and a modest increase, is how many plans end up working.

A payoff date is a plan, not a contract. Each year, compare your statement balance with the schedule, and re-run the calculation if you changed the payment, received a windfall, or refinanced. If your balance is ahead of schedule, you may be able to finish earlier than planned at the same payment.

items: Using the original loan amount or a rounded balance. The date depends on the current balance, so refresh the numbers with each statement.
Forgetting to mark extra money as principal-only. If it is applied to a future payment, it may not shorten the loan.
Skipping the safety net. A paid-down mortgage cannot be turned back into cash easily, so keep an emergency reserve and clear higher-rate debt first.

Ignoring that interest saved equals your loan rate. Money kept elsewhere could earn more or less. Returns are uncertain, and past performance does not guarantee future results, so weigh the trade-off rather than treating either choice as a rule.
Forgetting taxes and insurance. They sit outside principal and interest, and they can rise even as your loan shrinks.

sections.text: When these numbers do not apply

The figures assume a fixed rate, interest charged monthly, no prepayment penalty and extra money applied the day the payment is due. Adjustable-rate loans, loans with penalties, and plans that include selling the house within a few years behave differently. If you will sell soon, the interest you avoid is only what would have accrued until the sale. Use your own balance, rate, remaining term and payment in the Mortgage Payoff Calculator to see the exact payoff month.
